title: Wine and Strong Drink
lead: Wine was a staple of life in Bible lands, a sign of God's blessing and joy, a part of offerings and festivals, and the cup of the Lord's Supper. The Bible also warns sharply against drunkenness. Christians differ on whether believers may drink at all.

sections.h: Gift and danger in the Old Testament
sections.b: The Hebrew yayin is wine, and shekar, often translated "strong drink," was probably beer made from grain. Wine gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15) and was poured out as a drink offering (Numbers 15:5–10). Melchizedek brought out bread and wine to Abram (Genesis 14:18). Moses let worshipers spend their tithe money on "cattle, sheep, wine, beer, or anything else you would like" to feast before the LORD (Deuteronomy 14:26). Yet the first drunk in the Bible, Noah, is shamed (Genesis 9:20–23), and Lot's daughters get him drunk (Genesis 19:32–35). Priests were not to drink when they served at the sanctuary (Leviticus 10:9), and Nazirites gave up wine and anything from grapes during their vow (Numbers 6:3). Proverbs calls wine a mocker (Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35), and Isaiah condemns those who chase strong drink from morning on (Isaiah 5:11).
sections.refs: Psalm 104:15; Numbers 15:5–10; Genesis 14:18; Deuteronomy 14:26; Genesis 9:20–23; Genesis 19:32–35; Leviticus 10:9; Numbers 6:3; Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35; Isaiah 5:11; Jeremiah 35:1–19

sections.b: Jesus's first sign was turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana (John 2:1–11). His critics called him a glutton and a drunkard because he ate and drank with sinners, unlike John the Baptist (Matthew 11:18–19). At the Last Supper he gave the cup as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). Paul tells believers not to get drunk on wine but to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), lists drunkenness among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:21), and requires church leaders not to be given to much wine (1 Timothy 3:3, 8). He also tells Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21).
sections.refs: John 2:1–11; Matthew 11:18–19; Luke 22:20; Ephesians 5:18; Galatians 5:21; 1 Timothy 3:3–8; 1 Timothy 5:23; Romans 14:21

sections.b: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and many Reformed Christians hold that wine is a good gift to be used with self-control, and they use wine in the Lord's Supper. They teach that drunkenness is a sin, not drinking itself. In the 1800s the temperance movement led many Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal and other evangelical churches to ask members to abstain, citing the harm alcohol does and Paul's concern for the weaker brother; many of them use grape juice at communion. Wesley's General Rules already forbade drunkenness and drinking spirits except when needed. Adventists ask members to avoid alcohol for the sake of health and holiness, and Latter-day Saints abstain under the Word of Wisdom (Doctrine and Covenants 89). A minority argue that the "wine" the Bible approves was unfermented juice; most scholars think biblical wine was fermented.

common: Christians agree that drunkenness is sin and that believers should not cause others to stumble.
uncommon: Some abstainers hold that the wine Jesus made at Cana and used at the Last Supper was unfermented grape juice.
